content.title: About
content.content: Baby Toddler cereal is a whole‑grain infant cereal designed for children from 6 months old. It contains easily digestible grains, vitamins and minerals essential for growth and development. The cereal is free from artificial colours, flavours and gluten.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Made from whole oats and rice grains.
Includes pre‑biotics that support a healthy gut microbiome.
Product undergoes strict quality control and meets international infant‑food safety standards.
Packaging is made from recyclable material, reducing environmental impact.
Each serving provides a balanced ratio of carbohydrates, protein and fat.

items.title: Supports bone growth
items.content: Enriched with calcium and vitamin D, which help build strong bones.

items.title: Brain development
items.content: B‑vitamins and iron aid nervous system development and cognitive function.

items.title: Digestive health
items.content: Pre‑biotics and soluble fibre promote regular bowel movements and gut health.

items.title: Immune support
items.content: Vitamin C and zinc contribute to a robust immune system.

items.title: Energy provision
items.content: Complex carbohydrates provide sustained energy for active toddlers.

items.title: Grain allergy
items.content: Children with known oat, rice or other grain allergies should consult a pediatrician before use.

items.title: Over‑consumption
items.content: The cereal is calorie‑dense; follow the recommended serving size to avoid excess intake.

items.title: Choking hazard
items.content: For infants under 6 months, the cereal may be too thick; thin it to a smooth consistency.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Prepare the cereal with warm water or breast milk to the desired consistency. You can add fruit or vegetable puree for extra flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the package in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, use within 30 days and keep the bag tightly sealed.

content.title: About
content.content: Bread is a baked product made from dough of flour, water, yeast (or sourdough starter) and salt. It is a staple source of carbohydrates in many cultures and comes in many varieties: white, whole‑grain, rye, baguette, ciabatta, and more.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The earliest known bread was baked over 14,000 years ago in the Near East.
The word “bread” derives from the Proto‑Indo‑European root *bʰleh₁‑ meaning “to grow, to flourish”.
In ancient Rome, bread was a symbol of prosperity and often depicted on coins.
There are more than 200 recognized types of bread, differing in ingredients, leavening method, and shape.
Sourdough bread contains probiotic bacteria that may support gut health.

items.title: Source of complex carbohydrates
items.content: Bread provides steady energy by slowly releasing glucose into the bloodstream.

items.title: Rich in fiber (whole‑grain)
items.content: Whole‑grain breads contain dietary fiber that aids digestion and promotes satiety.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: B1, B2, B3 and folate support metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Mineral content
items.content: Bread supplies iron, magnesium, zinc and selenium.

items.title: Supports gut microbiota (sourdough)
items.content: Sourdough breads carry live cultures that can help balance intestinal microbiota.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: White bread can cause rapid spikes in blood sugar, which may be problematic for diabetics.

items.title: Gluten
items.content: People with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity should avoid regular wheat bread.

items.title: Salt content
items.content: Some breads contain high amounts of salt, potentially contributing to elevated blood pressure.

items.title: Preservatives and additives
items.content: Commercially produced loaves may include additives that are not suitable for everyone.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Bread can be enjoyed on its own, used for sandwiches and toast, served alongside soups and salads, or incorporated into breadcrumbs, croutons, and stuffing recipes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store bread in a cool, dry place in a paper bag or bread box. For longer storage, freeze in an airtight bag and thaw at room temperature.

content.title: About
content.content: Red velvet cake or cupcake is a tender dessert with a vivid red color, achieved by adding food coloring and a small amount of cocoa powder. It is traditionally made from a buttery batter flavored with vanilla and buttermilk, and finished with a rich cream cheese frosting.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first red velvet recipes appeared in the United States in the 1920s.
The bright red hue comes from a combination of cocoa powder and a touch of food coloring, sometimes beet juice.
Classic frosting is a cream cheese‑based buttercream.
In Russia the dessert is often served as individual cupcakes rather than a full‑size cake.
The contrast between the chocolate‑tinged crumb and sweet frosting enhances the flavor experience.

items.title: Source of protein
items.content: The batter contains eggs and dairy, providing a complete source of protein.

items.title: Calcium and vitamin D
items.content: Milk and cream cheese supply calcium and vitamin D, important for bone health.

items.title: Small amount of iron
items.content: Cocoa powder adds a modest amount of dietary iron.

items.title: Mood‑boosting effect
items.content: Sweet treats like red velvet can trigger endorphin release, improving mood.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Red velvet cakes and cupcakes are typically high in sugar, which can contribute to weight gain and tooth decay.

items.title: Allergy to dairy and eggs
items.content: Contains milk, cream cheese, and eggs, which may cause allergic reactions in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Trans fats in some recipes
items.content: If margarine is used instead of butter, trans fats may be present.

items.title: Food colorings
items.content: Certain artificial colorings can cause sensitivity in some people.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the cake in slices, often with an extra dollop of cream cheese frosting. Cupcakes are convenient as a snack; keep them refrigerated and enjoy them cold or slightly warmed.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the finished cake or cupcakes in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 5 days. For longer storage, freeze in a freezer‑safe bag for up to 2 months. Bring to room temperature before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Banana pepper (Capsicum annuum) is a long, slightly curved sweet‑pepper variety that resembles the shape of a banana. It has a mild, slightly sweet flavor and a crunchy texture. The pepper is eaten raw in salads, sandwiches, and as a garnish.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The name comes from its banana‑like shape.
It is one of the sweetest sweet‑pepper varieties, virtually free of heat.
Unlike many peppers, banana pepper is most often used fresh rather than roasted.
It is rich in vitamin C – one medium pepper provides over 150 % of the daily value.
The bright color attracts birds, helping to disperse its seeds.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C supports the immune system, collagen synthesis, and acts as an antioxidant.

items.title: Contains vitamin A and carotenoids
items.content: Carotenoids promote eye health and healthy skin.

items.title: Low‑calorie food
items.content: A medium pepper contains about 30 kcal, making it an excellent choice for weight‑controlled diets.

items.title: Source of dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion and contributes to a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Provides potassium
items.content: Potassium helps regulate fluid balance and supports heart function.

items.title: Nightshade allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to peppers, such as itching, swelling, or hives.

items.title: Pesticide residues
items.content: If the pepper is not organic, it should be washed thoroughly before consumption.

items.title: Digestive discomfort
items.content: Large amounts of raw pepper can cause gas or bloating in people with sensitive stomachs.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Banana pepper can be eaten raw in salads, sliced into sandwiches, used as a garnish for meat dishes, or added to vegetable platters. A light sprinkle of salt or a splash of lemon juice enhances its flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the pepper in the refrigerator’s vegetable drawer, wrapped in a perforated bag. When kept properly, it stays fresh for 1‑2 weeks. Discard any pepper that becomes soft, develops spots, or emits an off odor.

content.title: About
content.content: Shrimp are crustaceans from the Penaeidae family. In this product they are peeled, coated in a breadcrumb mixture and then baked or broiled. They have a delicate, slightly sweet flavor and a crisp outer crust.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Shrimp can grow up to 30 cm, but most market varieties are small (5–10 cm).
Coating is often made from wheat flour, breadcrumbs and spices, though gluten‑free versions exist.
Baking retains more nutrients than deep‑frying.
Shrimp are one of the fastest‑growing seafood species; they can be farmed in 3–4 months.
In some cultures shrimp are served cold, uncoated, as a “cocktail” with dipping sauce.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Shrimp provide about 20 g of high‑quality protein per 100 g serving.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: When baked, coated shrimp contain little fat, with most calories coming from protein.

items.title: Source of selenium
items.content: Selenium supports immune function and antioxidant protection.

items.title: Contains vitamin B12
items.content: Vitamin B12 is essential for nervous system health and red blood cell formation.

items.title: Rich in minerals
items.content: Shrimp supply zinc, iron and phosphorus, important for metabolism.

items.title: Shellfish allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience severe allergic reactions to shrimp.

items.title: Cholesterol content
items.content: Shrimp contain cholesterol, so people with high cholesterol should consume them in moderation.

items.title: Coating and trans fats
items.content: If the coating is made with partially hydrogenated oils, it may contain trans fats.

items.title: Microbial contamination
items.content: Improper storage can lead to bacterial growth and foodborne illness.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve hot as a main dish, slice into salads, add to pasta or rice. They are easy to eat with fingers, but can also be cut into bite‑size pieces. Pair with lemon, garlic, herbs or a light yogurt‑based sauce for extra flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep frozen coated shrimp at –18 °C. After thawing, store in the refrigerator for no more than 2 days and cook promptly. Do not leave at room temperature for more than 2 hours.

content.title: About
content.content: Whole grain waffles are a ready‑to‑cook frozen product made from whole wheat, oat or rye grains. They contain more fiber and nutrients than traditional waffles made with refined flour and retain the natural taste of the grain.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Whole grain waffles are typically produced without artificial colors or flavors.
Freezing preserves most B‑vitamins and minerals found in whole grains.
They can be quickly prepared in a toaster or oven, making them a convenient breakfast or snack option.
Whole grains are considered healthier because they keep the bran and germ intact.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: The whole grains provide dietary fiber that supports digestive health and promotes satiety.

items.title: Contains complex carbohydrates
items.content: Complex carbs release energy slowly, helping maintain stable blood‑sugar levels.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Waffles contain thiamine, riboflavin, niacin and folate, which are essential for metabolism.

items.title: Provides minerals
items.content: They supply magnesium, iron and zinc, important for muscle function and immunity.

items.title: Low in trans fats
items.content: When produced correctly, whole grain waffles contain little to no trans fats, making them heart‑friendlier.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: The product contains wheat, so it is unsuitable for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Some varieties may have added salt; those monitoring sodium intake should check the label.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: While less calorie‑dense than white‑flour waffles, they still provide a notable amount of energy and can contribute to weight gain if over‑consumed.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Toast the frozen waffles in a toaster, oven or microwave until golden and crisp. Serve with berries, yogurt, nut butter or a drizzle of honey. They can also be cubed and added to salads or soups for extra crunch.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the waffles in the freezer at –18 °C (0 °F) or lower. After thawing, use within 2–3 days and store in an airtight container in the refrigerator.
